analysis.one_liner: Bars federal district judges from issuing injunctions that apply nationwide or outside their own district.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal district judges sometimes issue 'nationwide injunctions' — orders that block a federal policy for everyone, not just the people who sued. This bill would amend federal law so a judge's injunction could bind only the parties in that case, or only people in that judge's district. That means a policy a judge finds unlawful could stay in force everywhere else in the country unless other people file their own lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: The sitting administration and parties defending federal policies: they would face, at most, an injunction limited to one case or one judicial district, so an unlawful policy could remain in effect for the rest of the country. Regulated industries and other litigants challenging or defending sweeping federal actions would also gain from narrower court orders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal agencies and parties defending policies

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits a district court from issuing any injunction unless it applies only to the parties before that court or only to that judicial district [S2][S3].

This would end the practice of a single district judge halting a federal policy nationwide, a power critics in both parties have called overreach, and would push other affected people to file their own suits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People harmed by a federal policy outside the judge's district would lose their fastest remedy: a single court order stopping the policy for everyone. Each group of affected people would need to file its own lawsuit, at its own cost and pace, to get relief.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone else affected by unlawful federal policies

drawbacks.text: The core trade-off: limiting injunctions to parties or one district means a policy found unlawful in one case could keep operating everywhere else, leaving most affected people without relief until they sue separately [S2][S3].

Supporters of nationwide injunctions argue they are sometimes the only effective remedy — for example, when a federal policy would cause irreparable harm to millions scattered across the country, and party-by-party suits cannot undo the damage in time. The bill does not create an alternative mechanism for those cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem — a single district judge's order can set national policy, and plaintiffs shop for friendly judges — but it solves it by removing the remedy rather than reforming it. Without any alternative route to broad relief, the main practical effect would be to make it slower and more expensive for ordinary people to stop an unlawful federal policy, while making life easier for the government and regulated parties defending it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Cotton introduced the bill on September 11, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded, and the bill expired at the end of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, district courts keep their existing power to issue nationwide injunctions, which in recent years has been the tool courts used to halt federal policies affecting millions. Defenders of that judicial power are better off; the bill's aim of narrowing court remedies went unrealized.

for.name: Tom Cotton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit district courts to injunctions binding only the case's parties or its district.

against.name: Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: The Judiciary Committee, which he chaired, received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the record shows no action after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown.

industries.industry: Federal executive agencies and parties defending federal policies
industries.note: The bill would cap any adverse court order at one case or one district, so a policy blocked in court could keep operating nationwide. Ordinary people challenging federal action would bear the cost of filing suit themselves.

industries.industry: Nationwide regulated industries (banks, employers, immigration-related businesses)
industries.note: These industries are frequently on either side of nationwide injunction fights — sometimes seeking them to block rules, sometimes hit by them. The bill would cut both ways for them, narrowing whatever remedy they obtained from a friendly district judge.
